screens.title: Why continuous vulnerability management matters
screens.narratorSegment: Vulnerability management is a continuous lifecycle: identify, assess, prioritize, remediate, and verify. It matters because vulnerabilities are discovered constantly, and any unpatched host or image is a potential entry point for attackers. In an AWS DevOps environment the emphasis is on automation and repeatability. That means using inventory systems to know which instances and images exist, using automated scanners to assess them on a schedule, and applying fixes through scripted, auditable processes. A concrete example: an EC2 fleet with instances tagged by service that are automatically included in a patch group. Systems Manager applies approved security updates during a weekly maintenance window, Inspector runs scans after a rebuild, and Image Builder creates a new golden AMI if tests pass. A common misconception is thinking vulnerability management is a single task executed by operations staff. In reality it is cross-team: dev teams must produce safer images, security teams must define baselines and severity handling, and infrastructure teams must automate deployment of patched artifacts. The core takeaway is to treat vulnerability management as an automated program with pipelines, gates, and measurable milestones rather than ad hoc firefighting. How will you make vulnerability checks an automated milestone in your pipeline?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Why continuous vulnerability management matters
Definition & claim

Vulnerability management is the ongoing process of identifying, assessing, prioritizing, remediating, and verifying software and configuration vulnerabilities in systems and applications.

Identify: Inventory and automatic discovery of EC2 instances and images.
Assess: Automated scanning with Amazon Inspector and SCA tools for images and libraries.
Remediate: Apply patches or rebuild golden AMIs and replace instances.
Key Takeaway

Treat vulnerability management as an automated pipeline with verifiable gates, not a manual checklist.

Concrete example

Imagine a service deployed from images in ECR. After each push the CI pipeline triggers an Inspector scan on the image and an SCA scan on dependencies. If a high-severity vulnerability appears, the build fails and a ticket is created. When the package is fixed, Image Builder runs to create a new AMI and instances are replaced behind a load balancer.

Common misconception

Some teams assume running a scan once is sufficient. Vulnerability management must be continuous because new CVEs and dependency issues appear over time.

Check your understanding: Which step in the lifecycle lets you prevent vulnerable images from reaching production?

screens.title: Automated patching with AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Patch Manager automates applying operating system updates to managed instances, which can be EC2 or on-premises servers registered with Systems Manager. The core pieces to configure are a patch baseline, patch groups, and maintenance windows. A baseline contains approval rules that determine which classifications and severities to install and when. Patch groups are logical collections of instances, typically identified with a tag like PatchGroup: MyWebAppServers. Maintenance windows schedule when a Run Command task runs the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document so updates apply at predictable times. A concrete example: create a baseline that auto-approves security and bugfix updates after seven days, tag instances as MyWebAppServers, and schedule a weekly Sunday maintenance window at 02:00 UTC. A common mistake is not testing patches in a non-production environment before broad rollout; this creates regressions. Also avoid broad IAM permissions for SSM agents — follow least-privilege. The practical benefit is consistent, auditable patching that reduces variance across your fleet and enables reporting on compliance. How would you verify a baseline is applied across all instances in a patch group? Automated patching with AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager means baseline + patch group + maintenance window → repeatable, auditable os patching for managed instances.. In practical terms, define baselines, patch groups, and maintenance windows for reliable os updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Baseline + patch group + maintenance window → repeatable, auditable OS patching for managed instances.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Patch Manager
Process overview
  1. Author a patch baseline with approval rules for classifications and severities.
  2. Tag instances and map the tag to a patch group.
  3. Create a maintenance window and register a Run Command task using AWS-RunPatchBaseline.
Example baseline (conceptual)
# PatchBaselines:
- Name: "MyLinuxPatchBaseline"
  OperatingSystem: "AMAZON_LINUX_2"
  ApprovalRules:
    PatchFilters:
      - Key: "CLASSIFICATION"
        Values: ["Security", "Bugfix"]
      - Key: "SEVERITY"
        Values: ["Critical", "Important"]
    ApproveAfterDays: 7
  RejectedPatches: ["specific-patch-id-to-avoid"]
Concrete scenario

You tag web servers with PatchGroup: MyWebAppServers, add that group to the baseline, and schedule a weekly window. Systems Manager will run patches automatically and report compliance, so you can prove who and when updates were applied.

Common mistake

Skipping testing before broad deployment and granting overly permissive SSM roles. Both cause regressions or security gaps.

Key Takeaway

A declarative baseline plus scheduled windows turns manual updates into predictable automation.

screens.title: Patch baseline structure and common policy choices
screens.narratorSegment: A patch baseline defines which patches are approved for automatic installation and under what conditions. Typical policy choices include approving security and bugfix classifications quickly while deferring non-security updates, and only auto-approving critical and important severities after a short delay to allow initial testing. For example, you might auto-approve security updates seven days after release to let upstream regressions surface. A baseline can also include rejected patches for specific known-bad updates. When you combine baselines with patch groups, you obtain per-service policies: one group might accept automatic updates quickly for stateless test environments, while another delays patches for production. A common misconception is that shorter approval windows are always better; in practice a short delay balances rapid remediation with operational stability. Here’s a conceptual YAML baseline you can adapt as IaC. Use the console, CLI, or CloudFormation to implement it and always test on a subset of instances first. Patch baseline structure and common policy choices means approval rules let you tune speed versus stability: classifications, severities, and approval delays form the core policy knobs.. In practical terms, approval rules, classifications, severities, and delay windows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Patch Baseline Structure
Policy knobs explained
  • Classifications: security, bugfix, enhancement — choose which to auto-approve.
  • Severities: critical, important — often prioritized for quicker approval.
  • ApproveAfterDays: a delay to let initial patches settle in the ecosystem.
  • RejectedPatches: explicitly exclude problematic updates.
Pro tip

Use different baselines for production and non-production to balance stability and speed.

Conceptual baseline (read-only example)
# Example: Patch Baseline definition (conceptual)
PatchBaselines:
  - Name: "MyLinuxPatchBaseline"
    OperatingSystem: "AMAZON_LINUX_2"
    ApprovalRules:
      PatchFilters:
        - Key: "CLASSIFICATION"
          Values: ["Security", "Bugfix"]
        - Key: "SEVERITY"
          Values: ["Critical", "Important"]
      ApproveAfterDays: 7
    RejectedPatches: ["specific-patch-id-to-avoid"]
Do not paste this into production; adapt and test. Use least-privilege IAM for Systems Manager roles used by instances.

screens.title: Amazon Inspector: automated vulnerability assessments
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Inspector performs automated security assessments of EC2 instances and container images stored in ECR. It discovers software packages, compares them to known vulnerability databases, and reports findings with severity and remediation guidance. For DevOps, the most valuable pattern is integrating Inspector into CI/CD so images are scanned before promotion and AMIs are assessed after build. A concrete example: after pushing an image to ECR the pipeline triggers an Inspector vulnerability assessment for that image; if a high-severity finding is present the pipeline blocks deployment until remediation. A common misconception is thinking Inspector replaces patching; instead Inspector detects issues that you must remediate through patching or rebuilding images. Findings can be consumed programmatically to create tickets, raise alerts, or trigger automated remediation workflows using EventBridge and Lambda. The practical benefit is catching vulnerabilities earlier and providing structured remediation instructions so fixes are smaller, safer, and trackable. What criteria would you set to fail a build based on an Inspector finding? In practical terms, scan ec2 instances and ecr images and act on findings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Amazon Inspector
What Inspector does
  • Discovers packages and configuration issues on EC2 and in ECR images.
  • Generates findings with severity and remediation guidance.
  • Integrates with automation via EventBridge for alerts and actions.
Key Takeaway

Inspector helps you shift vulnerability detection left and provides structured findings for programmatic remediation.

Pipeline integration example
# Example: Trigger an Inspector scan for an ECR image (CLI)
# This is often integrated into a CodePipeline stage after image push
aws inspector2 start-software-vulnerability-assessment --resource-arn arn:aws:ecr:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:repository/my-app-repo/image/my-app-image:latest
When a finding appears, you can fail the pipeline or route the finding to a remediation workflow. Inspector is detection — remediation is patching or rebuilding images.

screens.title: EC2 Image Builder and golden AMIs
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 Image Builder enables you to define image recipes that include a base image, hardening components, installation steps, and tests. The architecture pattern here is immutable infrastructure: rather than patching running servers, you rebuild a golden AMI and replace instances. A typical flow: Image Builder pulls a base image, applies hardening scripts and security agents, runs automated tests, then publishes a new AMI. You then roll that AMI into your Auto Scaling groups or replacement process. The advantage is reproducibility and simpler rollback: if a new AMI causes problems you launch the previous AMI. A frequent mistake is failing to include automated tests in the image pipeline; without tests you risk shipping regressions. Another misconception is thinking Image Builder replaces patching entirely — it complements patching by ensuring new instances begin in a patched, hardened state. In practice, pair Image Builder with Inspector scans and patch manager reports so you have visibility on both built images and running instances. How might you design your rollout to minimize user impact while replacing instances with new AMIs? EC2 Image Builder and golden AMIs means use image builder to produce tested, hardened amis that replace mutable instances and simplify rollbacks.. In practical terms, bake, test, and deploy immutable images for consistent environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › EC2 Image Builder
Image Builder workflow
  1. Select base image and define components (agents, packages, hardening).
  2. Run build and automated tests in the pipeline.
  3. Publish the AMI and deploy via replacement or Auto Scaling.
Example test
Verify that security agents are running, that the kernel is updated, and that a smoke test of the application succeeds before publishing.
Operational benefits
  • Immutable instances reduce configuration drift.
  • Rollbacks are simpler: launch prior AMI versions.
  • Image tests enforce quality gates before deployment.
Key Takeaway

Bake security into images and automate validation so new instances launch in a known-good state.

screens.title: Patching running instances vs. rebuilding images
screens.narratorSegment: There are two dominant approaches to keeping software current: patch running instances in place or rebuild images and replace instances. Patching running instances is often faster for emergency fixes and uses tools like Patch Manager to schedule updates. However, it introduces configuration drift because each instance may diverge over time. Rebuilding images with Image Builder and replacing instances favors immutability: every new server starts from the same hardened AMI. This simplifies rollbacks and testing but requires discipline in CI/CD to automate rebuilds and redeployments. A concrete example: a critical CVE requires a kernel update. Quick mitigation might use Patch Manager to apply the kernel patch to running hosts. For a longer-term approach you would update your Image Builder recipe, build a new AMI, and replace instances behind a load balancer. A common misconception is that immutable images remove the need for patching entirely. In reality, patching still applies to running hosts until all are replaced and Image Builder outputs are updated continuously. Choose a hybrid strategy: use Patch Manager for short-term fixes and Image Builder for long-term consistency. Which approach would you adopt for stateful databases and why?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Patch vs Rebuild
Patching running instances
  • Fast response for critical fixes.
  • Can be automated with Patch Manager and maintenance windows.
  • Risk: configuration drift and inconsistent state.
Rebuilding images (immutable)
  • Consistent, repeatable images produced by Image Builder.
  • Simpler rollbacks by deploying previous AMIs.
  • Requires deployment pipelines that replace instances safely.

screens.title: Managing third-party software and dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: Third-party libraries and open-source components can introduce critical vulnerabilities into your applications. Managing these dependencies requires a combination of tooling and process. Software Composition Analysis tools scan dependency manifests during the build to identify known vulnerable packages. The chapter mentions tools like Snyk and OWASP Dependency-Check as examples of this practice; the important point is to scan during the build phase so you fail fast. Regularly updating dependencies reduces exposure; consider using automated dependency update tools in your repository. Supply chain security means trusting package sources and verifying integrity — use trusted registries and checksums when possible. A common mistake is focusing only on OS-level patches and ignoring application libraries. Another is assuming that updating a library is risk-free; you must test updates in non-production environments. A practical workflow: add an SCA stage in CI that fails the build on high-severity findings, notify the developer team, and create a ticket. This keeps remediation close to the authors who can evaluate compatibility and test changes. How will you make SCA results actionable for your team? screens.title: Activity: Automating patching with Patch Manager
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through automating patching for Amazon Linux 2 instances using Systems Manager. Start by launching an EC2 instance with an IAM instance profile that grants the managed instance the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy so it appears in Systems Manager inventory. Verify the SSM Agent is running and that the instance is listed as a managed instance. Next, create a custom patch baseline for Amazon Linux 2 configured to auto-approve Security and Bugfix classifications after seven days; set this as the default baseline for that OS. Tag your instance with PatchGroup: MyWebAppServers and create a patch group that maps to this baseline. Optionally run AWS-RunPatchBaseline manually to simulate patching now and observe command execution status and compliance reports. A common mistake is forgetting to test these steps on a small set of instances. Always validate results in a non-production environment first. screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: Teams commonly make several recurring mistakes when implementing vulnerability management. First, relying on manual patching at scale leads to inconsistency and missed updates; automation with Patch Manager is necessary. Second, ignoring scan results is a frequent operational failure — scan findings must be prioritized and assigned. Third, using outdated AMIs or not including AMI rebuilds in your pipeline allows drift to reintroduce vulnerabilities. Fourth, granting overly broad permissions to SSM agents or automation roles creates new attack surfaces; always apply least privilege. Fifth, not testing patches or image changes in non-production environments leads to avoidable outages. As a safety note, automated remediation should be limited to well-understood, reversible actions; complex changes require human review and clear rollback plans. A helpful practice is to maintain an incident playbook that lists which findings can be auto-remediated and which require manual intervention. The bottom line is to combine automation with careful controls, testing, and clear ownership so speed does not become a source of risk. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we’ll build a clear, operational view of vulnerability management for AWS workloads. You will learn how to stop relying on manual updates and instead create automated, repeatable patching and image-building workflows that fit inside infrastructure as code and CI/CD pipelines. We’ll cover Systems Manager Patch Manager so you can approve and schedule OS patches reliably, Amazon Inspector so you can scan instances and images automatically, and EC2 Image Builder so you can produce golden AMIs that eliminate drift. Along the way we’ll discuss how to manage third-party libraries with software composition analysis and how to design continuous scanning and automated remediation triggers. By the end you’ll understand both the tools and the practices: why baselines and maintenance windows matter, how to shift vulnerability checks left in the build, and how immutable images simplify rollbacks. A practical walkthrough ties these pieces together: tagging an instance, creating a patch baseline, scheduling a maintenance window, and running a scan. Keep an eye out for common mistakes such as ignoring scan findings or using overly broad permissions. Ready to see concrete examples and hands-on steps that you can reproduce in your pipelines?

Across these objectives you will gain skills for automating patching, scanning images, creating hardened AMIs, and managing third-party dependencies. First, you will implement automated patching for EC2 using Systems Manager Patch Manager: this means defining a baseline, grouping instances, and scheduling maintenance windows so updates apply reliably. Second, you'll learn to use Amazon Inspector to run automated vulnerability assessments against EC2 instances and container images. That includes interpreting severity, filtering findings, and using results as gate checks in a pipeline. Third, you'll create secure, hardened AMIs with EC2 Image Builder so instances launch from a known-good, patched state. Fourth, you'll develop strategies for third-party software and dependency management using software composition analysis during builds. Each objective ties to verifiable milestones such as creating a patch baseline, enabling an Inspector scan on an image, producing a tested Image Builder recipe, and integrating an SCA scan into a build. These practical skills matter because they convert policy into repeatable automation that scales beyond manual updates and reduces human error.

In this second objectives slide we focus on operational integration and continuous remediation. You will learn to create patch groups and maintenance windows so updates are applied at predictable times with minimal disruption. You will practice integrating Inspector scans into CI/CD pipelines, enabling 'shift left' detection of vulnerable images before they reach production. You will design rebuild-and-replace workflows using Image Builder to keep AMIs current and to support immutable deployments, including planning rollbacks. Finally, you will implement continuous scanning and automated remediation strategies using events and small automation functions. Each objective includes a tangible verification: tagging instances into patch groups, adding an Inspector stage in the pipeline, producing a rebuilt AMI from Image Builder, or wiring an automated remediation action when a critical finding appears. These objectives help you move from one-off fixes to a continuous program that reduces exposure and scales across teams.

Vulnerability management is a continuous lifecycle: identify, assess, prioritize, remediate, and verify. It matters because vulnerabilities are discovered constantly, and any unpatched host or image is a potential entry point for attackers. In an AWS DevOps environment the emphasis is on automation and repeatability. That means using inventory systems to know which instances and images exist, using automated scanners to assess them on a schedule, and applying fixes through scripted, auditable processes. A concrete example: an EC2 fleet with instances tagged by service that are automatically included in a patch group. Systems Manager applies approved security updates during a weekly maintenance window, Inspector runs scans after a rebuild, and Image Builder creates a new golden AMI if tests pass. A common misconception is thinking vulnerability management is a single task executed by operations staff. In reality it is cross-team: dev teams must produce safer images, security teams must define baselines and severity handling, and infrastructure teams must automate deployment of patched artifacts. The core takeaway is to treat vulnerability management as an automated program with pipelines, gates, and measurable milestones rather than ad hoc firefighting. How will you make vulnerability checks an automated milestone in your pipeline?

Patch Manager automates applying operating system updates to managed instances, which can be EC2 or on-premises servers registered with Systems Manager. The core pieces to configure are a patch baseline, patch groups, and maintenance windows. A baseline contains approval rules that determine which classifications and severities to install and when. Patch groups are logical collections of instances, typically identified with a tag like PatchGroup: MyWebAppServers. Maintenance windows schedule when a Run Command task runs the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document so updates apply at predictable times. A concrete example: create a baseline that auto-approves security and bugfix updates after seven days, tag instances as MyWebAppServers, and schedule a weekly Sunday maintenance window at 02:00 UTC. A common mistake is not testing patches in a non-production environment before broad rollout; this creates regressions. Also avoid broad IAM permissions for SSM agents — follow least-privilege. The practical benefit is consistent, auditable patching that reduces variance across your fleet and enables reporting on compliance. How would you verify a baseline is applied across all instances in a patch group? Automated patching with AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager means baseline + patch group + maintenance window → repeatable, auditable os patching for managed instances.. In practical terms, define baselines, patch groups, and maintenance windows for reliable os updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A patch baseline defines which patches are approved for automatic installation and under what conditions. Typical policy choices include approving security and bugfix classifications quickly while deferring non-security updates, and only auto-approving critical and important severities after a short delay to allow initial testing. For example, you might auto-approve security updates seven days after release to let upstream regressions surface. A baseline can also include rejected patches for specific known-bad updates. When you combine baselines with patch groups, you obtain per-service policies: one group might accept automatic updates quickly for stateless test environments, while another delays patches for production. A common misconception is that shorter approval windows are always better; in practice a short delay balances rapid remediation with operational stability. Amazon Inspector performs automated security assessments of EC2 instances and container images stored in ECR. It discovers software packages, compares them to known vulnerability databases, and reports findings with severity and remediation guidance. For DevOps, the most valuable pattern is integrating Inspector into CI/CD so images are scanned before promotion and AMIs are assessed after build. A concrete example: after pushing an image to ECR the pipeline triggers an Inspector vulnerability assessment for that image; if a high-severity finding is present the pipeline blocks deployment until remediation. A common misconception is thinking Inspector replaces patching; instead Inspector detects issues that you must remediate through patching or rebuilding images. Findings can be consumed programmatically to create tickets, raise alerts, or trigger automated remediation workflows using EventBridge and Lambda. The practical benefit is catching vulnerabilities earlier and providing structured remediation instructions so fixes are smaller, safer, and trackable. EC2 Image Builder enables you to define image recipes that include a base image, hardening components, installation steps, and tests. The architecture pattern here is immutable infrastructure: rather than patching running servers, you rebuild a golden AMI and replace instances. A typical flow: Image Builder pulls a base image, applies hardening scripts and security agents, runs automated tests, then publishes a new AMI. You then roll that AMI into your Auto Scaling groups or replacement process. The advantage is reproducibility and simpler rollback: if a new AMI causes problems you launch the previous AMI. A frequent mistake is failing to include automated tests in the image pipeline; without tests you risk shipping regressions. Another misconception is thinking Image Builder replaces patching entirely — it complements patching by ensuring new instances begin in a patched, hardened state. In practice, pair Image Builder with Inspector scans and patch manager reports so you have visibility on both built images and running instances. There are two dominant approaches to keeping software current: patch running instances in place or rebuild images and replace instances. Patching running instances is often faster for emergency fixes and uses tools like Patch Manager to schedule updates. However, it introduces configuration drift because each instance may diverge over time. Rebuilding images with Image Builder and replacing instances favors immutability: every new server starts from the same hardened AMI. This simplifies rollbacks and testing but requires discipline in CI/CD to automate rebuilds and redeployments. A concrete example: a critical CVE requires a kernel update. Quick mitigation might use Patch Manager to apply the kernel patch to running hosts. For a longer-term approach you would update your Image Builder recipe, build a new AMI, and replace instances behind a load balancer. A common misconception is that immutable images remove the need for patching entirely. In reality, patching still applies to running hosts until all are replaced and Image Builder outputs are updated continuously. This hands-on activity guides you through automating patching for Amazon Linux 2 instances using Systems Manager. Start by launching an EC2 instance with an IAM instance profile that grants the managed instance the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy so it appears in Systems Manager inventory. Verify the SSM Agent is running and that the instance is listed as a managed instance. Next, create a custom patch baseline for Amazon Linux 2 configured to auto-approve Security and Bugfix classifications after seven days; set this as the default baseline for that OS. Tag your instance with PatchGroup: MyWebAppServers and create a patch group that maps to this baseline. Then create a maintenance window, for example weekly on Sunday at 02:00 UTC, and register a Run Command task that uses AWS-RunPatchBaseline targeting PatchGroup: MyWebAppServers. Optionally run AWS-RunPatchBaseline manually to simulate patching now and observe command execution status and compliance reports. A common mistake is forgetting to test these steps on a small set of instances. Always validate results in a non-production environment first. After completing the activity, reflect on how you will integrate these steps into your infrastructure-as-code pipelines.

Teams commonly make several recurring mistakes when implementing vulnerability management. First, relying on manual patching at scale leads to inconsistency and missed updates; automation with Patch Manager is necessary. Second, ignoring scan results is a frequent operational failure — scan findings must be prioritized and assigned. Third, using outdated AMIs or not including AMI rebuilds in your pipeline allows drift to reintroduce vulnerabilities. Fourth, granting overly broad permissions to SSM agents or automation roles creates new attack surfaces; always apply least privilege. Fifth, not testing patches or image changes in non-production environments leads to avoidable outages. As a safety note, automated remediation should be limited to well-understood, reversible actions; complex changes require human review and clear rollback plans. A helpful practice is to maintain an incident playbook that lists which findings can be auto-remediated and which require manual intervention. The bottom line is to combine automation with careful controls, testing, and clear ownership so speed does not become a source of risk.
